title: Keys, Roman numerals, and progressions
summary: Read key signatures, name the chords in a key with Roman numerals, and play I–IV–V–I and I–V–vi–IV with smooth voice leading.

lessons.title: Keys and key signatures
lessons.summary: What a key is, how key signatures work, and the circle of fifths.

steps.title: What a key is
steps.body:
A piece is **in a key** when it uses mostly the notes of one scale and sounds "at home" on that scale's tonic. A song in G major uses the G major scale (with F♯) and tends to end on G.

Instead of writing ♯ on every F, sheet music puts a **key signature** at the start of each staff line: the sharps or flats that apply to every note of that letter, in every octave, throughout the piece.

steps.title: Common major keys
steps.body:
| Key | Signature | Sharps or flats |
|---|---|---|
| C major | none | — |
| G major | 1 sharp | F♯ |
| D major | 2 sharps | F♯ C♯ |
| A major | 3 sharps | F♯ C♯ G♯ |
| F major | 1 flat | B♭ |
| B♭ major | 2 flats | B♭ E♭ |

Sharps always appear in the order **F C G D A E B**; flats in the reverse order, **B E A D G C F**.

Shortcuts for major keys:
- **Sharp keys:** the tonic is a half step above the last sharp (last sharp C♯ → D major).
- **Flat keys:** the tonic is the second-to-last flat (B♭ E♭ → B♭ major). One flat is F major.

diagram.caption: D major key signature: F♯ and C♯.

steps.title: The circle of fifths
steps.body:
Arrange the keys so each is a **perfect 5th** above the last: C → G → D → A → E → B …. Each step clockwise **adds one sharp**. Going the other way (down a 5th each time: C → F → B♭ → E♭ …) **adds one flat**.

Neighbors on the circle share all but one note, which is why music often moves between them.

diagram.caption: Clockwise adds sharps; counterclockwise adds flats.

exercise.prompt: Play A major with the right hand, A3 to A4 and back (three sharps: F♯, C♯, G♯). Fingering is the same as C major: up 1 2 3 1 2 3 4 5.
exercise.rhythm: q q q q q q q q q q q q q q h

mistakeTips: C♯ (finger 3) is the first black key; the thumb then passes under to D.
F♯ (finger 3) and G♯ (finger 4) are both black keys.
Every F, C, and G in this key is sharp.

questions.prompt: How many sharps are in D major?
questions.explanation: D major: F♯ and C♯.

questions.prompt: Which key has one flat?
questions.explanation: F major has B♭.

questions.prompt: What is the order of sharps?
choices: F C G D A E B
B E A D G C F
C G D A E B F
F G A B C D E
questions.explanation: Flats run in the reverse order.

questions.prompt: Moving clockwise on the circle of fifths…
questions.explanation: C → G (1 sharp) → D (2 sharps)…

questions.prompt: A key signature with F♯, C♯, and G♯ is which major key?
questions.explanation: A half step above the last sharp (G♯) is A.

reviewItems.answer: F C G D A E B

lessons.title: Chords in a key: Roman numerals
lessons.summary: Build a triad on every degree of a major scale and label it with a Roman numeral.

steps.title: Diatonic triads
steps.body:
**Diatonic** means "using only the notes of the key." Build a triad on each degree of a major scale and you always get the same pattern of qualities:

**major, minor, minor, major, major, minor, diminished**

Musicians label them with **Roman numerals**: uppercase = major, lowercase = minor, lowercase with ° = diminished.

**I ii iii IV V vi vii°**

steps.title: The same numerals in four keys
steps.body:
| | I | ii | iii | IV | V | vi | vii° |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| C | C | Dm | Em | F | G | Am | B° |
| G | G | Am | Bm | C | D | Em | F♯° |
| D | D | Em | F♯m | G | A | Bm | C♯° |
| F | F | Gm | Am | B♭ | C | Dm | E° |

Roman numerals let you describe a progression once and play it in any key. The **I** (tonic) sounds like home, **V** (dominant) pulls strongly back to I, and **IV** (subdominant) moves away from home more gently.

steps.title: The diatonic triads of G major
steps.caption: G, Am, Bm, C, D, Em, F♯°, G.

exercise.prompt: Right hand 1 3 5: play every diatonic triad in G major from G4: G, Am, Bm, C, D, Em, F♯°, G.

mistakeTips: Every F is F♯ in G major, so Bm is B D F♯ and D is D F♯ A.
Keep the hand frame and move one key at a time.

questions.prompt: In C major, what is the vi chord?
questions.explanation: The 6th degree is A; the triad A C E is minor.

questions.prompt: In G major, what is the V chord?
questions.explanation: The 5th degree of G is D; D F♯ A is major.

questions.prompt: In F major, what is the IV chord?
questions.explanation: The 4th degree of F major is B♭; B♭ D F is major.

questions.prompt: What does lowercase "ii" tell you?
choices: The chord on degree 2 is minor
The chord on degree 2 is major
questions.explanation: Uppercase = major, lowercase = minor.

questions.prompt: Which degree has the diminished triad in a major key?
questions.explanation: vii°: B D F in C major.

reviewItems.prompt: Triad qualities in a major key, I to vii°?
reviewItems.answer: major, minor, minor, major, major, minor, diminished

reviewItems.prompt: I, IV, and V in G major?
ii, iii, and vi in F major?

lessons.title: I–IV–V–I with smooth voice leading
lessons.summary: The most common progression in Western music, with the closest right-hand inversions.

steps.title: A progression
steps.body:
A **progression** is a sequence of chords. **I–IV–V–I** moves from home (I) away (IV) to tension (V) and back home (I). The move V→I is called a **cadence**: a musical resting point.

Play it with the closest inversions so the hand hardly moves:

- **C major:** C (C4 E4 G4) → F/C (C4 F4 A4) → G/B (B3 D4 G4) → C (C4 E4 G4)
- **G major:** G (G4 B4 D5) → C/G (G4 C5 E5) → D/F♯ (F♯4 A4 D5) → G (G4 B4 D5)

Notice the **common tones**: C stays through C and F/C; G stays through C and G/B.

diagram.caption: C → F/C → G/B → C, right hand.

steps.title: I–IV–V–I in C
steps.caption: Closest right-hand inversions, with the bass note in the left hand.

exercise.prompt: Right hand: C → F/C → G/B → C, repeating, for 60 seconds.

mistakeTips: RH fingering: C = 1 3 5, F/C = 1 3 5 (C F A), G/B = 1 2 5 (B D G).
Keep the thumb on C for the first two chords, then move it down a half step to B.
Say the Roman numerals as you play: one, four, five, one.

exercise.prompt: Right hand in G major: G → C/G → D/F♯ → G, repeating, for 60 seconds.

mistakeTips: The thumb stays on G4 for G and C/G, then moves down to F♯4 for D/F♯.

steps.title: Adding the 7th: V7
steps.body:
The **dominant seventh** chord (**V7**) adds a 4th note to V, a minor 7th above the root. In C major, **G7 = G B D F**. Its F pulls down to E, and its B pulls up to C, which makes V7→I even more final.

A close right-hand version from F/C: **B3 F4 G4** (leave out D). C→B, F stays, A→G. Then resolve to C (C4 E4 G4).

questions.prompt: In D major, I–IV–V–I is…
questions.explanation: I = D, IV = G, V = A.

questions.prompt: In F major, what is V7?
questions.explanation: The 5th degree of F is C; the dominant seventh is C E G B♭.

questions.prompt: Which note do C and F/C share?
questions.explanation: C E G and C F A share C.

questions.prompt: A cadence is…
choices: A musical resting point, such as V→I
questions.explanation: V→I is the strongest cadence.

questions.prompt: Listen. Which progression is this?
questions.explanation: Home, away, tension, home.

questions.prompt: Listen. Is the last chord I or V?
questions.explanation: It ends on the tension chord, which wants to return home.

reviewItems.prompt: Closest RH inversions for I–IV–V–I in C?
reviewItems.answer: C4 E4 G4 → C4 F4 A4 → B3 D4 G4 → C4 E4 G4

lessons.title: I–V–vi–IV
lessons.summary: A four-chord progression heard in countless pop songs, played with smooth inversions.

steps.title: Four chords
steps.body:
**I–V–vi–IV** is one of the most-used progressions in pop music. In C major: **C – G – Am – F**. In G major: **G – D – Em – C**.

Closest right-hand voicings:

- **C:** C (C4 E4 G4) → G/B (B3 D4 G4) → Am/C (C4 E4 A4) → F/C (C4 F4 A4)
- **G:** G (G4 B4 D5) → D/F♯ (F♯4 A4 D5) → Em/G (G4 B4 E5) → C/G (G4 C5 E5)

Each change moves at most one or two notes by a step, and at least one note stays put.

steps.title: I–V–vi–IV in C
steps.caption: With a left-hand bass note on each root.

exercise.prompt: Right hand: C → G/B → Am/C → F/C, repeating, for 60 seconds.

mistakeTips: G/B uses fingers 1 2 5; Am/C and F/C use 1 3 5 or 1 2 5, whichever keeps your hand still.
From G/B to Am/C every note moves up one step: B→C, D→E, G→A.
Aim for no gap between chords.

exercise.prompt: Right hand in G: G → D/F♯ → Em/G → C/G, repeating, for 60 seconds.

mistakeTips: The top note goes D5 → D5 → E5 → E5.
Em/G = G4 B4 E5; C/G = G4 C5 E5.

questions.prompt: I–V–vi–IV in G major is…
questions.explanation: I = G, V = D, vi = Em, IV = C.

questions.prompt: I–V–vi–IV in F major is…
questions.explanation: I = F, V = C, vi = Dm, IV = B♭.

questions.prompt: What is Am/C?
questions.explanation: A minor (A C E) with C in the bass.

questions.prompt: Listen. Which progression is this?
questions.explanation: Home, dominant, relative minor, subdominant.

steps.title: Roman numerals: I, IV, V, vi
